Provocation
prov-oh-KAY-shun
n.
From Latin provocare, to call forth, to challenge. Webster 1828: the act of provoking; anything that excites anger. In Scripture the provocation, with the article, is a proper name for one place and one day — Meribah, where Israel tempted God at the rock, and which Hebrews makes the standing warning to the church.

Biblical Definition

The provocation is a technical term. Psalm 95 gives it: Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, and as in the day of temptation in the wilderness (Psalm 95:8), where the Hebrew has the place-names Meribah and Massah — strife and testing — the water from the rock at Rephidim and again at Kadesh. The writer to the Hebrews takes that psalm and preaches it twice to Christians: Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness (Hebrews 3:8), and again at Hebrews 3:15, with the whole warning of chapters 3 and 4 built on it. The offence is stated by God Himself as unbelief in the face of evidence: How long will this people provoke me? and how long will it be ere they believe me, for all the signs which I have shewed among them? (Numbers 14:11). That is the anatomy of provocation. It is not the sin of a man who has seen nothing; it is the sin of a people who came through the sea, ate the manna daily, and still asked whether God was among them. Hebrews draws the application without softening it: those bodies fell in the wilderness, and they could not enter in because of unbelief.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PROVOCATION as the act of provoking; anything that excites anger; and, in law, an appeal to a higher court. The Latin root means to call forth or summon — provocation calls anger out of the one provoked.

PROVOCATION, n. — The act of provoking; anything that excites anger or resentment.

The cause of resentment; that which stirs up displeasure.

In law, an appeal to a superior court — the original Latin sense of calling forth.

In Scripture, the provocation with the definite article denotes the events at Meribah and Massah (Exodus 17; Numbers 20).

The Hebrew place-names carry the meaning: Meribah is strife or chiding, and Massah is temptation or testing.

Key Scripture

Psalm 95:8 — "Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, and as in the day of temptation in the wilderness:"

Hebrews 3:8 — "Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness:"

Hebrews 3:15 — "While it is said, To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation."

Numbers 14:11 — "And the LORD said unto Moses, How long will this people provoke me? and how long will it be ere they believe me, for all the signs which I have shewed among them?"

Isaiah 53:5 — "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed."

Modern Corruption

Hebrews 3 and 4 are the classic Arminian proof texts for the loss of salvation, and the classic ground of easy-believism’s embarrassment; the Reformed reading takes the warning at full strength precisely because perseverance is a doctrine about the means God uses.

expand to see more

The warning is real, and any exposition that blunts it has failed. Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God. The Reformed answer is not that the warning is hypothetical but that warnings are among the means by which God keeps His own. The same chapter that says the elect cannot finally fall also says exhort one another daily, while it is called To day — and the exhortation is the instrument. A man who hears Hebrews 3, is alarmed, and holds fast is exhibiting the perseverance the doctrine describes; a man who hears it, shrugs, and hardens is showing what he always was. The wilderness generation is the standing case: they had every external privilege of the covenant and no faith, and Hebrews says the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it.

The opposite abuse is the easy-believism that treats the warning as irrelevant to anyone who once made a decision. Numbers 14:11 exposes it. God’s complaint is not that Israel had never professed; it is that after the plagues, the sea, the pillar, and the manna they still would not believe Him. Repeated exposure to God’s works without trust does not produce neutrality. It produces hardness, and hardness is cumulative — which is why the text says To day three times. The provocation was not one bad afternoon. It was ten temptings, and the sentence when it fell was forty years long.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Meribah (H4809), strife, and Massah (H4532), temptation — the place-names Psalm 95:8 uses; Greek parapikrasmos (G3894), a bitter provocation, in Hebrews 3.

expand to see more

Hebrew Meribah (H4809) — strife, chiding; the place named at Exodus 17:7 and Numbers 20:13.

Hebrew Massah (H4532) — temptation, testing; the companion name at Exodus 17:7.

Hebrew na’ats (H5006) — to spurn, to provoke, to despise; how long will this people provoke me? (Numbers 14:11).

Greek parapikrasmos (G3894) — provocation, embitterment; Hebrews 3:8, 15, occurring nowhere else in the New Testament.

Greek skleruno (G4645) — to harden; harden not your hearts, the same verb used of Pharaoh in the Septuagint.

Usage

"Harden not your heart, as in the provocation (Psalm 95:8) — Meribah made a permanent warning."

"How long will it be ere they believe me? (Numbers 14:11) — God’s own diagnosis of the offence."

"As in the provocation (Hebrews 3:15) — the wilderness preached to the church, twice in one chapter."
